title: Customer data archival, snapshot, and restore requirements for private deployments
author: Maya Chen
body:
Summary

This document captures the minimum customer-facing requirements and acceptance criteria for data archival, snapshotting, and restore workflows for Redwood private deployments (VPC and on-prem). It is intended to be used during procurement, onboarding, and operational handoffs so that engineering, SRE, and customer-success agree on retention windows, encryption, verification cadence, and automated restore proof points.

Goals
- Define required archival targets and snapshot frequency for control-plane and runtime state.
- Specify security, integrity, and compliance constraints for snapshot storage.
- Provide clear acceptance tests and runbook steps for restore verification during on-boarding and periodic audits.
- Provide example automation patterns and API/CLI snippets customers can run in acceptance tests.

Scope
- Applies to private deployment artifacts managed by Redwood: model artifacts (serving bundles), KV cache checkpoints (sharded), runtime metadata (tenant routing tables), and control-plane configuration (policies, secrets metadata).
- Excludes customer application data stored outside Redwood runtime (e.g., user DBs).
- Covers both VPC-hosted and fully air-gapped on-prem installations where network egress may be restricted.

Definitions
- Snapshot: point-in-time copy of runtime state sufficient to restore service to an operational state without re-running lengthy rebuilds (e.g., model weights are separate immutable blobs, snapshot captures pointers and runtime caches).
- Archive: long-term retention store for compliance/e-discovery where data is kept for regulatory reasons and may not be immediately accessible for restore without rehydration.
- Restore window: the expected end-to-end time to bring a tenant or control-plane service back to operational readiness from a snapshot.

High-level requirements
1) Retention and frequency
   - Control-plane configuration snapshots: full snapshot every 24 hours, incremental every 4 hours. Retention: 180 days standard; configurable up to 7 years.
   - Runtime KV cache checkpoints: snapshot every 6 hours; retention 30 days.
   - Model-serving metadata (version pins, rollout state): snapshot every 1 hour; retention 90 days.
   - Audit and telemetry indices required for incident investigation: archival weekly, retention per customer contract (default 365 days).

2) Encryption and integrity
   - All snapshots and archived objects MUST be encrypted at rest using customer-managed keys (CMK) where customer requests; otherwise default to FIPS-140-2 compliant KMS.
   - Snapshots must include a signed manifest with SHA-256 checksums for each object. Redwood tooling will verify checksum on write and periodic verification.

3) Access controls and separation
   - Snapshot read and restore operations require an RBAC role distinct from routine operator roles (e.g., snapshot-reader, snapshot-restorer).
   - Restore operations that access customer PII must trigger an approval workflow logged to the audit trail and require at least two approvers when confidentiality is high.

4) Storage targets and placement
   - Supported sinks: S3-compatible object stores (MinIO, AWS S3, GCS via interop layer), NFS for air-gapped environments (with manifests stored separately), and removable offline archives on encrypted volumes for extreme airgap workflows.
   - Snapshots SHOULD be stored in at least two availability zones or two independent physical vaults for on-prem airgapped sites (e.g., onsite + encrypted tape or offline vault).

5) Restore SLAs and verification
   - For control-plane snapshots: restore window <= 60 minutes for full control-plane to basic operational state (excluding model weight rehydration).
   - For tenant-level runtime restore (stateless model serving plus KV caches): warm restore <= 30 minutes (KV rehydration may be best-effort background process).
   - Every restore must include integrity validation: manifest checksum comparisons, post-restore smoke tests (token-level generation against sample prompts), and a routing sanity check.

Acceptance test matrix (table)
| Component | Snapshot cadence | Retention | Restore window (target) | Validation steps |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Control-plane config | 24h full / 4h incremental | 180d | <=60m | manifest verification, reconcile policies, API health checks |
| Runtime KV cache (per-tenant) | 6h | 30d | <=30m | checksum, sample inference requests, cache hit-rate sanity |
| Model-serving metadata | 1h | 90d | <=30m | version pin assertions, canary route verification |
| Telemetry indices | weekly archive | 365d | N/A (rehydration may be slow) | sample query, index integrity check |

Operational runbook: snapshot creation
1. Pre-checks:
   - Verify target storage is reachable and has >= 20% free space or cold-archive capacity.
   - Ensure KMS key policy grants Redwood snapshot service encrypt/decrypt for CMK operation.
2. Execute snapshot job:
   - CLI (example):
     redwoodctl snapshot create --scope control-plane --type full --target s3://customer-snapshots/tenant-123/$(date +%F)
   - Job outputs a signed manifest and a job id: SR-<timestamp>. Log the job id to customer handoff.
3. Post-checks:
   - Wait for checksum verification step to complete (redwoodctl snapshot verify --job SR-12345).
   - Send webhook notification to customer-specified URL on success or failure.

Operational runbook: restore (high-level)
1. Authorization:
   - Open a change request with snapshot id, reason, approvers, and expected impact window.
   - Get approval per customer policy; document approvers and timestamp.
2. Dry-run verify:
   - redwoodctl snapshot inspect --id SR-12345 --verify-manifest-only
   - If manifest verification fails, escalate to SRE.
3. Restore execution:
   - redwoodctl snapshot restore --id SR-12345 --scope tenant:tenant-123 --mode warm --target-cluster cluster-a
   - Monitor restore progress via /internal/restore/jobs/<job-id> and watch metrics restore.progress and restore.errors.
4. Post-restore validation:
   - API health checks (expected endpoints): /health, /v1/generate sample prompt, KV hit rate > baseline threshold.
   - Run a 5-minute canary traffic stream (configured in the runbook) to validate latency and correctness.

Automation examples
- Periodic verification job (YAML for orchestrator):
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: CronJob
  metadata:
    name: redwood-snapshot-verifier
  spec:
    schedule: "0 */6 * * *"  # every 6 hours
    jobTemplate:
      spec:
        template:
          spec:
            containers:
            - name: verifier
              image: redwood/ops-tools:stable
              args: ["snapshot", "verify", "--recent=48h"]
            restartPolicy: OnFailure

- Sample S3 lifecycle policy (JSON) for warm-to-cold tiering:
  {
    "Rules": [
      {
        "ID": "move-to-cold-after-30d",
        "Filter": {"Prefix": "tenant-123/"},
        "Status": "Enabled",
        "Transitions": [{"Days": 30, "StorageClass": "GLACIER"}],
        "Expiration": {"Days": 3650}
      }
    ]
  }

Monitoring and alerting
- Alerts to configure in customer/operator alerting stack:
  - SnapshotFailureRate > 1% over 1 hour -> page SRE (P1).
  - VerifyJobChecksumMismatch -> page SRE (P2) and alert customer ops channel.
  - StorageAvailable < 15% -> warn customer ops and create automatic retention review ticket.

Validation checklist for customer sign-off
- Snapshot schedule configured and created in writable storage accessible to customer and Redwood.
- CMK or equivalent KMS integration tested and decrypts snapshots in staging restore.
- Run at least two successful restores in a staging region or airgapped test environment: one control-plane and one tenant-level.
- Post-restore smoke tests pass (endpoints respond, sample generation within expected latency band).
- Audit entries recorded for each snapshot/restore operation and exported to customer audit sink for retention.

Roles and responsibilities
- Customer-success: coordinate acceptance tests, record approvals, and confirm policy choices for retention and KMS.
- SRE/Field-ops: execute snapshot/restore, run verification jobs, and troubleshoot checksum or storage failures.
- Security & Compliance: approve any retention longer than 3 years and validate archived data classification controls.
- Customer: provide target storage credentials, outbound webhook endpoints, and approved approvers for restores.

Edge cases and special considerations
- Airgapped sites: snapshots may be written to local encrypted volumes with manifest transfer out-of-band. Acceptance tests must include a manifest-only remote verification step and an offline restore drill.
- Large model rehydration: model weights are typically gigabytes; acceptance criteria should allow model rehydration to be asynchronous with snapshot restore if model blobs are stored in a separate immutable registry.
- Legal holds: when legal hold applies, retention policies must override automatic deletion; implement a ‘hold’ flag on snapshot objects.

Appendix A — Example acceptance test script (bash)
#!/usr/bin/env bash
SNAP_ID=$(redwoodctl snapshot create --scope control-plane --type full --target s3://customer-snapshots/test/$(date +%s) | jq -r .jobId)
redwoodctl snapshot verify --job $SNAP_ID || { echo "Snapshot verification failed"; exit 2; }
RESTORE_JOB=$(redwoodctl snapshot restore --id $SNAP_ID --scope tenant:test-tenant --mode warm --target-cluster test-cluster | jq -r .jobId)
# Wait loop (simple)
for i in {1..60}; do
  STATUS=$(redwoodctl restore status --job $RESTORE_JOB | jq -r .status)
  if [[ "$STATUS" == "completed" ]]; then
    echo "Restore completed"; break
  fi
  sleep 30
done
# Run smoke test
curl -s -X POST https://test-cluster.redwood/api/v1/generate -d '{"prompt":"health check"}' | jq -r .choices[0].text

Appendix B — Common failure modes and remediation
- Manifest checksum mismatch: run incremental verification, if persistent, mark snapshot as corrupted and use previous snapshot; escalate for forensics.
- KMS permission denied: validate key policy, ensure Redwood service principal is included, and replay the successful snapshot in staging.
- Slow restore due to network saturation: throttle parallel restore workers or move restore target to a local registry and rehydrate models separately.
